extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students studying ordinary differential equations (ODEs)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook-level solution methods and existence criteria for homogeneous linear ordinary differential equations: (a) constant-coefficient scalar equations and first-order systems (characteristic polynomial, multiplicities, Jordan form, matrix exponential), and (b) second-order linear equations solved by power-series and Frobenius (regular) singular-point methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic polynomial and exponential solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The polynomial P(λ) obtained from the linear differential operator is called the characteristic polynomial; L(e^{r t}) = P(r) e^{r t} shows that y(t)=e^{r t} is a solution of L(y)=0 if and only if r is a root of the characteristic polynomial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor P(λ) into linear factors (over C). Distinct roots and multiplicities determine the form and number of fundamental solutions. Use P(r)=0 to identify exponential solutions ert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity yields polynomial-times-exponential solutions (Lemma 4.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (d/dt - r)^m (y) = 0 (m≥1), then the functions e^{r t}, t e^{r t}, ..., t^{m-1} e^{r t} are solutions of this mth-order differential equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct differentiation verifies these are solutions. Thus a root r of multiplicity m of the characteristic polynomial produces m linearly independent solutions of the form t^k e^{r t}, k=0,...,m-1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear independence of generalized exponential solutions (Lemma 4.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If r1,..., rN are distinct complex numbers and m_j are positive integers, then the collection of functions e^{r_j t}, t e^{r_j t}, ..., t^{m_j-1} e^{r_j t} (for j=1..N) are linearly independent over C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via induction on N using differentiation and degree arguments for polynomials multiplying exponentials. This establishes that different root chains provide independent solution vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis of solutions for nth-order constant-coefficient equation (Proposition 4.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For y^{(n)} + a_{n-1} y^{(n-1)} + ... + a_0 y = 0 with characteristic polynomial P(λ)=∏_{j=1}^k (λ - r_j)^{m_j}, the n functions e^{r_j t}, t e^{r_j t}, ..., t^{m_j-1} e^{r_j t} (for j=1..k) form a basis of the solution space over C on any interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine Lemma 4.10 (they are solutions), Lemma 4.11 (they are independent), and dimension theorem (solution space dimension = n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real coefficients produce real-valued solution bases
rubrics_metrics.description: If the differential equation has real coefficients, complex-conjugate roots occur in pairs and the real and imaginary parts of complex-valued solutions are real-valued solutions; replace e^{(a±bi)t} and their t^k-multiples by t^k e^{a t} cos(bt) and t^k e^{a t} sin(bt) to obtain a real basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closure under complex conjugation and linear independence over C to conclude linear independence over R. This gives a real-valued basis of the real solution space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix exponential gives fundamental solutions for linear systems
rubrics_metrics.description: For the system y' = A y with constant n×n matrix A, each column of e^{tA} is a solution; the n columns are linearly independent at t=0 and form a basis of solutions on any interval. The solution satisfying y(t0)=y0 is y(t)=e^{(t-t0)A} y0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical computation of e^{tA} is not obvious in general; use Jordan form or model cases where the exponential series can be summed entrywise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model cases for computing e^{tA} (Jordan blocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three model computations: (1) a nilpotent Jordan block C (zeros below main diagonal) yields e^{tC} upper triangular with entries t^k/k!; (2) a Jordan block A=aI+C gives e^{tA}=e^{at} e^{tC}; (3) block-diagonal matrices with Jordan blocks yield e^{tA} block-diagonal with block exponentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These model cases show how to form e^{tA} when A is in Jordan form; they are the building blocks for the general computation via similarity transform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan normal form existence (Theorem 4.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any square complex matrix A there exists a nonsingular complex matrix B such that B^{-1} A B = J is in Jordan form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J is unique up to permutation of Jordan blocks; B is not unique. The theorem reduces computation of e^{tA} to computing e^{tJ} via model cases and then transforming back by B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic polynomial determines diagonal entries of Jordan form
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic polynomial det(λ I - A) equals det(λ I - J); its factorization into linear factors determines the diagonal entries (eigenvalues) of J and their multiplicities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the polynomial gives eigenvalues and algebraic multiplicities, it does not by itself determine Jordan block sizes; further kernel-dimension data are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining Jordan block sizes via null-space dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The sizes and counts of Jordan blocks for eigenvalue a are determined by the sequence of dimensions dim ker(A - a I)^k for k=1,2,... . Specifically, these kernel dimensions encode the numbers of Jordan blocks of each size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute successive nullities of (A - aI)^k; differences between these dimensions give the number of blocks of each size. This information together with eigenvalues determines J.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing the similarity matrix B from chains of generalized eigenvectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Columns of B are chosen as chains of generalized eigenvectors Bei satisfying (A - aI) Bei = previous vector in chain; start from largest k (max power for which kernel grows) and build bases Sk of ker(A - aI)^k with consistency so that images under (A - aI) link the chains properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic construction: choose basis S_k of largest kernel, extend backwards by applying (A - aI) to obtain consistent bases S_{k-1}, etc.; order columns to reflect chain order (e.g., Av1, v1, v2...). The resulting B gives B^{-1} A B = J.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power-series (analytic) coefficient theorem for second-order linear ODEs (Theorem 4.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P(t) and Q(t) are given by convergent power series for |t|<R, then any formal power series satisfying y'' + P(t) y' + Q(t) y = 0 actually converges for |t|<R. Consequently every solution on (-R,R) is given by a power series convergent for |t|<R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute y(t)=∑ c_n t^n, obtain recursive relations determining c_n from c_0 and c_1 (which are arbitrary and correspond to initial values y(0), y'(0)). Use bounding and ratio-type estimates to prove convergence on |t|<R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive determination of Taylor coefficients at ordinary points
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting a power series into y'' + P(t)y' + Q(t)y = 0 yields coefficient equations forcing c_0 and c_1 to be arbitrary and recursively determining c_2, c_3, ... from previous coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This matches existence-uniqueness: c_0=y(0), c_1=y'(0). In practice the recursion can become complicated; sometimes closed-form expressions appear in special cases (e.g., Legendre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legendre equation special-case criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For Legendre's equation (1-t^2) y'' - 2t y' + p(p+1) y = 0, the recurrence for coefficients leads to a closed-form product expression; when p is a nonnegative integer, one solution becomes a polynomial of degree p (Legendre polynomial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the general power-series method or ratio test for convergence; observe numerator factors vanish for integer p producing termination (polynomial solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular singular point and Frobenius method (indicial equation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For t^2 y'' + t P(t) y' + Q(t) y = 0 with P,Q analytic (regular singular at t=0), seek solutions of the form t^s (c_0 + c_1 t + ...) with c_0 ≠ 0. The exponent s must satisfy the indicial equation s(s-1) + a_0 s + b_0 = 0 (where a_0,b_0 are constant terms of P,Q expansions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once s is chosen, c_0 arbitrary and recursion determines c_n provided the denominator ( (n+s)(n+s-1) + a_0 (n+s) + b_0 ) ≠ 0 for all n≥1. Failure of denominators corresponds to resonances and may force logarithmic terms or other phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence cases for Frobenius solutions (Proposition 4.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If the indicial equation has distinct roots that do not differ by an integer, then for each root s there is a formal solution t^s(c_0 + c_1 t + ...). (b) If the roots differ by an integer, there is always a 1-parameter family of solutions associated to the larger root, and the smaller root may produce a solution or require special handling (log terms) analogous to the Euler equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summarizes which formal Frobenius series are guaranteed and flags the resonance (integer-difference) complication. When roots differ by an integer additional analysis is needed to determine the second independent solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of Frobenius (regular singular) formal series (Theorem 4.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P(t) and Q(t) are analytic for |t|<R, then every formal Frobenius series solution t^s(c_0 + c_1 t + ...) converges for 0 < |t| < R to an actual solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses bounds and induction analogous to the ordinary-point case, choosing radii r<R and estimating coefficients to show uniform bounds yielding convergence on (0,R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler equation as prototype for regular singular behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Euler equation t^2 y'' + t P y' + Q y = 0 with constant P,Q, substitute y=t^s to obtain the algebraic (indicial) equation s(s-1)+P s+Q=0; distinct roots give power-law solutions t^{s_1}, t^{s_2}, a double root yields solutions t^s and t^s log t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example motivates Frobenius method: change of variables or seeking t^s series transforms regular singular problems into constant-coefficient-like algebraic indicial equations and clarifies possible log-term behavior in the resonance/double-root cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bessel equation and special-function construction
rubrics_metrics.description: For Bessel's equation t^2 y'' + t y' + (t^2 - p^2) y = 0 the indicial roots are s=±p; the series solution with s=p yields the Bessel function J_p(t) defined by an explicit convergent power series (J_p(t) = (t/2)^p / Γ(p+1) times a power series). If p is integer or half-integer special phenomena occur for the second solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute recursion from the Frobenius substitution; use ratio test for convergence. Be aware of complications when p is integer (second solution involves logarithms or the Neumann function).
